source.title: Breaking Safety at the Token Boundary: How BPE Tokenization Creates Exploitable Gaps in LLM Alignment
source.authors: Tung-Ling Li; Hong-Liang Liu; Yuhao Wu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study tests a token-fragmentation mechanism and shows that flipping the first-token refusal signal does not reliably produce harmful behavior, qualifying the claim that getting past an opening defeats safety. Its attacks and measurements do not test the specific interventions or metrics named in V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own experiments on BPE fragmentation, first-position logit gaps, harmful outputs, layer localization, and fine-tuning defenses. These results do not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant prefilling, suffix attacks, decoding changes, or safety localized in weights/ranks. The cited claims and findings from other papers are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: Rows r6–r9 show that flipping the first-token refusal decision (via input BPE fragmentation, greedy decoding) yields harmful output in only 29–65% of cases (YES+PARTIAL). That qualifies V4's idea that getting past the opening defeats refusal. The attack is an input perturbation, not prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes, so the link to V4 is indirect. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The 48% 'harmful' figure counts YES+PARTIAL (only 18% are YES). SFT closed ASR on 3/5 families, but only through global collapse that also raised refusal on benign prompts. The authors frame their result as the input-side cause consistent with Qi et al.'s output-side shallow-alignment diagnosis.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies character-level BPE fragmentation, first-position logit gaps, activation patching, dataset scans, and SFT/DPO defenses. It does not use the original studies' fine-tuning intervention or per-token KL measurement recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Space insertion produces stronger gap effects than tested Unicode perturbations (mean |∆Gap| 1.07 versus 0.48); attack outcomes vary by model; behavioral judgments vary by judge (up to 18pp absolute ASR spread); defense conclusions depend on training recipe, pool size, and seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: Greedy space insertion flipped the first-token refusal gap on 80–100% of refused HarmBench prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BPE fragmentation of safety-critical input tokens can flip a first-position refusal trigger.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation patching gives model-dependent layer recovery patterns (concentrated in Qwen/Gemma, distributed in Llama/Mistral), at n=20 with wide CIs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fragmentation disrupts refusal-gap computation through model-dependent layer pathways. This is layer-level evidence, not weight- or rank-level localization.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal-target SFT/DPO with fragmented augmentation: DPO gives no seed- and pool-stable ASR closure; SFT lowers ASR on some families only through global over-refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under LoRA-16, adding fragmented refusal data does not selectively repair fragmentation jailbreaks.

record.code_released: Code and aggregate outputs will be released upon publication; no URL stated.
record.problems: The alignment-data scan uses public datasets as proxies, not the evaluated models' proprietary training data. The main scope is five model families at 4–8B plus one 72B probe; HarmBench is the harmful-prompt benchmark. Activation patching uses n=20 with reported CI half-widths of ±16–21pp, and tokenizer family co-varies with patching pattern at n=5. The defense tests use LoRA rank 16; Qwen3 and Gemma DPO results remain pool-confounded. ASR judging is not human-calibrated; absolute estimates vary by up to 18pp across judges, although the paper says cell rankings are stable.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; 24 rows retained, below the 60-row limit. Other reported analyses, including word-completion probes and perturbation-type sweeps, were not extracted because they do not measure a listed claim version and are not needed to represent the central first-token trigger, behavioral outcome, layer, and fine-tuning findings.

untested.parts: Compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes and decoding changes are not tested. Only input-side fragmentation that flips the first-token logit gap is tested.
No benign fine-tuning measured for safety erosion. The A.8 pilot on PKU 'chosen' responses is safety-adjacent data, not benign data.
No per-token KL across response positions. Table 3 compares base and instruct only at the first position.
Layer-level patching only; no weight or rank localization.
Gives an input-distribution explanation, not an account of output-position shallowness.
No training that spreads safety across response positions.

missing.what: Per-model ROC-AUC of first-token gap polarity versus behavioural refusal (0.66–0.98, pooled 0.84). Bears on how far the first-token decision determines behaviour.
First-token refusal gap in base versus instruct models (base raw +1.6 to +2.6, instruct +9.0 to +15.7). First-position aligned-vs-base difference only, no other positions.
missing.versions: V3 (first position only; cannot show concentration)

record.verdict_notes: V4 link is indirect: the first token is bypassed by input fragmentation, not by prefilling. The judge saw responses truncated to 300 characters, which may undercount later harm. Judge calibration was done on Llama only, with ±18pp spread across judges.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning experiment uses a few to a few hundred harmful examples as harmful-compliance targets and measures the resulting safety loss.
No experiment fine-tunes on ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data to measure its effect on harmful compliance.
The paper measures a first-position logit gap, not per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
The attacks fragment input text; the study does not test compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways of passing response-opening tokens.
Layer contributions and activation patching are measured, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
The study probes a data-distribution explanation for input-fragmentation vulnerability, not why aligned-versus-base output distributions are shallow across response positions.
The training experiments do not train safety across response positions or test whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: Five 4–8B instruct models; greedy space-insertion input attack flips the first-token gap; greedy decoding; Gemini judge on truncated responses
relationships.reason: After the opening refusal token is bypassed, only 48% of 167 responses were harmful (per model 29–65%); the rest avoided harm downstream (r6–r9).
relationships.display_finding: After the opening refusal token is bypassed, only 48% of 167 responses are harmful (29–65% per model); the rest avoid harm later in the response.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
